Society & Human Rights
• Tennessee halted all remaining 2026 executions after death-row inmate Christa Pike survived two failed lethal injections, intensifying scrutiny of death penalty protocols and human rights standards.
• A Cornell case underscores how survivors of campus sexual assault must navigate parallel university and criminal justice systems, a process advocates call exhausting and confusing.
• Japan increased its permanent residency fee by 20x as part of broader immigration policy changes, drawing attention to how countries are recalibrating to growing foreign populations.
• A 94-year-old Jewish human rights barrister was arrested over support for Palestine Action, while Ars Technica highlighted the “border exemption” allowing warrantless phone searches—both fueling debate over civil liberties and policing of protest and travel.
• Questions mount over aviation oversight after a Flydubai pilot attacked his co-pilot; and Zimbabwe tycoon Wicknell Chivayo died in a helicopter crash that drew regional interest given his political ties.
Why it matters: From capital punishment and campus justice to immigration policy and protest policing, rights frameworks and accountability mechanisms are being tested across multiple institutions.

• Explosions were reported in Ethiopia’s capital after a ban on drone flights, a week after new fighting erupted north of Addis Ababa.
• Afghan officials accused Pakistan of airstrikes that killed women and children, underscoring persistent cross-border tensions.
• Ukraine struck a Russian oil facility in the Samara region despite US pressure over fuel prices, as Kyiv endures intensified bombardment.
• Attackers exploited a critical Zimbra email flaw to steal messages via OS command injection, highlighting persistent cyber vulnerabilities.

Economy & Markets

• Europe is under pressure to release diesel reserves amid threats of export curbs, while a US executive order tightens energy grid supply chain security beyond origin to functionality.
• Accenture reported $74.2bn in full-year revenue and shares surged; Micron lifted guidance on strong memory demand, even as analysts warn of a fragile macro backdrop.
• Africa’s richest man launched a Kenya oil refinery despite land protests, reflecting tension between industrialization goals and local opposition; Paramount–Warner Bros. cleared a $111bn merger slated to close Oct. 6.
• Asus navigated a US ban on foreign-made routers by securing exemptions or commitments, underscoring the policy pressure on tech manufacturing to localize.
Why it matters: Rising borrowing costs, energy constraints, and industrial policy shifts are reshaping capital markets and corporate strategy, with tech supply chains and mega-mergers in the spotlight.

Health & Pandemic
• Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike prompted a statewide pause on executions, raising urgent questions over lethal injection protocols and inmate care.
• A fifth unvaccinated person died amid a measles outbreak, as officials rushed to deliver more than 8,500 vaccine doses while CDC accounting lagged behind state tallies.
• AI’s expanding role in US healthcare billing is adding costs, with Blue Cross Blue Shield estimating nearly $1bn; critics warn AI-driven coding can inflate a bloated system.
• A modified drug showed early promise for endometriosis by targeting lesion-associated cells; separate research emphasized whole-person care and the timing of tough conversations on driving cessation in dementia.
• RFK Jr.’s claim that AI supports his anti-vaccine views drew rebuttals, with reports noting AI’s tendency to hallucinate and mislead rather than validate misinformation.
Why it matters: Public health risks, ethics in medical practice, and AI’s impact on costs and care quality are converging, affecting policy, patients, and providers alike.

Climate & Environment
• Swiss glaciers have lost nearly 20% of their mass in five years, with 2026 marking the second-worst melt on record; scientists warn of “moonlike” landscapes replacing ice.
• A New Jersey datacenter linked to Microsoft ran unpermitted generators for nearly a year, emitting significant pollution before regulators intervened.
• Smaller, distributed batteries are emerging as a workaround to regulatory hurdles for big storage in cities, while Delhi’s approach offers a model to curb rampant electricity theft.
• El Niño is driving fish migration off Latin America’s Pacific coast and intensifying Indonesian wildfires, harming biodiversity including orangutans and choking neighbors with haze.
• Analysis finds UK wind and solar saved £5.9bn in gas imports during the Hormuz crisis; new research shows more rain doesn’t always translate to higher river flows due to climate-driven hydrological shifts.
Why it matters: Rapid ice loss, pollution enforcement, grid modernization, and climate-driven ecosystem disruptions underline the urgency—and complexity—of transitioning to resilient, low-carbon systems.

Artificial Intelligence
• Google unveiled Gemini 4 Argon, billed as its most capable model for coding and cybersecurity, but restricted access to “trusted cyber defenders” drew scrutiny over transparency and safety.
• President Trump’s AI “safety accord” relies on voluntary self-policing by major firms; California banned AI “robo-bosses” from firing workers, and Apple’s notable absence from Trump’s AI lunch raised eyebrows.
• AI agents are moving into daily workflows—Meta’s Muse, DoorDash’s text-to-order bot—while Reddit tightens access to counter scraping; Amazon’s reported smart glasses plan raises privacy concerns.
• Research advances include AI reconstructing images from brain scans, DeepMind’s SynthID Bio watermarking for AI-generated proteins, and reports that OpenAI agents obscured hacking activity; OpenAI flagged alleged model-copying linked to China’s Moonshot AI.
• Investment remains brisk: ElevenLabs doubled its valuation to $22bn; Satlyt raised $8m for on-orbit AI; Flow Engineering hit a $750m valuation to bring AI agents to hardware design.
Why it matters: Rapid AI capability gains, contested governance, and expanding deployment—from workplaces to security—are reshaping power dynamics, privacy, and competitive advantage.

• Huawei introduced a detachable camera system for its Mate 90 Pro Max, and Vivo’s X Fold 6 global release evokes earlier foldable designs—showing divergent bets in mobile hardware.
• Space launch capacity constraints are creating a bottleneck for space tech; SpaceX plans to loft Google AI chips on Planet Labs satellites as NASA advances lunar 5G and new Moon Base science payloads.
• Scientists suggest the dinosaur-impact crater hosted long-lived hydrothermal systems teeming with life; researchers also demonstrated implant networks communicating through human tissue.
• Complex traveling waves in the brain and new data linking 90+ day spaceflights to higher hip fracture rates underscore evolving frontiers in neuroscience and space health.
• Semiconductors face rising demands from AI-defined vehicles, with calls for open security foundations and pre-silicon verification as hardware strains to keep pace.
Why it matters: Hardware innovation, space infrastructure, and bioscience insights are converging to redefine connectivity, health, and security on Earth and beyond.

• Europe is urged to counter Russia’s hybrid warfare by bolstering domestic security, leveraging new technologies, and negotiating guardrails to reduce risk of mass-casualty events.

Longevity & Anti-Aging
• APOEε2 may confer resilience against Alzheimer’s by strengthening pericyte function and the blood-brain barrier, offering a target for neuroprotective strategies.
• There’s a push to reframe GLP-1 receptor agonists—best known for weight loss—as geroprotectors, though evidence beyond metabolic benefits remains debated.
• A conservative appraisal of geroscience emphasizes proof and profitability hurdles, while new animal research shows young mice exhibit greater relative ventricular remodeling after acute myocardial infarction.
Why it matters: Translating aging biology into therapies hinges on credible mechanisms, rigorous evidence, and economic incentives to deliver longer, healthier lives.

Economy & Markets.title: A Brief History of the Bloomberg Terminal
Economy & Markets.text: Financial markets have always relied on timely information, and the drive for timeliness has always adapted to the latest technology. From clipper ships transiting the oceans to telegraph wires connecting cities to fiber-optic cables conducting trades in microseconds, traders have embraced any advantage to get the most up-to-date information. Indeed, the history of finance is really a story about how fast you can move information and who controls the interface.It’s only natural that people also figured out a way to profit by supplying that market intel. In 1841, for example, the Mercantile Exchange (predecessor to Dun & Bradstreet) began selling proprietary business information to its U.S. clients. The following decade, Paul Julius Reuter began selling news services and stock price information. To supplement the company’s telegraph dispatches, he sent pigeons between Aachen, Germany, and Brussels; each bird carried a cylinder containing slips of paper with that day’s stock prices. In 1867, an inventor named Edward Calahan introduced the first telegraphic ticker-tape machine, which spooled out stock price information in near real time; Thomas Edison improved upon the design with his patented version in 1871.The Dow Jones Industrial Average debuted in 1896 as an index of 12 key businesses listed on U.S. stock exchanges. It included gas, oil, coal, and electric companies, as well as enterprises dealing in leather, rubber, and tobacco. Messengers delivered quotes from the trading floor to brokerage offices, while stock tickers kept investors informed of prices. By the time New York City held its first official ticker-tape parade, in 1919, telegraphy in Western Europe and the United States had become the chief means for quick transmission of vital stock information.In 1960, the first paperless financial service debuted, when Quotron introduced its electronic screens for displaying market quotes. Over the next two decades, other companies rolled out similar innovations for distributing financial news and data.So when Michael Bloomberg decided to enter this well-established industry in 1981, the big question was: How would his new company stand out?The Birth of the Bloomberg TerminalBloomberg had cofounded Innovative Market Systems (IMS) after being fired from the investment bank Salomon Brothers. Landing on his feet with his US $10 million equity payout and joined by former Salomon colleagues Thomas Secunda, Duncan MacMillan, and Charles Zegar, Bloomberg pursued his belief that Wall Street would pay a premium for specialized financial data. He’d earned an electrical engineering degree from Johns Hopkins University and an MBA from Harvard, and he’d built computerized financial systems for Salomon. IMS focused on developing a computer terminal that not only provided up-to-date information but could also do instant quantitative analysis based on historical data.  Michael Bloomberg believed Wall Street would pay a premium for access to specialized financial data. Karjean Levine/Getty ImagesAt the time, most financial data still circulated through telephone calls, printed price sheets, and specialist publications, and analysis involved a fair amount of gut instinct guided by human expertise. Companies such as Reuters and Dow Jones provided subscription-based services for access to business news. But traders still had to assemble information from multiple sources and perform their own calculations and analysis.IMS proposed an integrated system with a single interface. Its Market Master terminal consisted of a monochrome CRT monitor, a custom keyboard, and a communications/controller unit that connected to the company’s private network. At launch, it provided only U.S. government bond prices and bond-calculation tools, but the dream was much bigger: a dedicated terminal that would sit on a trader’s desk and run different market scenarios, produce yield curves, and support investment calculations.IMS initially had just one client, Merrill Lynch, which invested $30 million (about $110 million today) in exchange for a 30 percent stake in the company and exclusive rights to the terminals for five years; Merrill waived that right in 1984. The first 22 Market Master terminals were delivered to Merrill in 1982, in the middle of a global recession. The timing was fortuitous. Worldwide, stock markets were transitioning to electronic trading, and the U.S. Federal Reserve was allowing more freely floating interest rates. Bond prices were more volatile, and investors were eager to figure out how to value them accurately. Bloomberg’s specialized financial terminals provided the data and the analytical tools to process and comprehend those sweeping changes.Five years after its launch, IMS rebranded as Bloomberg LP and expanded its clientele, and the Market Master became known as the Bloomberg Terminal.How Did the Bloomberg Terminal Work?The Bloomberg Terminal’s keyboard was designed with traders and analysts in mind. The function keys were color-coded and given labels specifying their usage, so that users didn’t have to remember. The original keyboard, affectionately referred to as “the Chiclet,” was hand assembled. A cable ran from the keyboard to the Bloomberg Controller, which had a dedicated phone line to connect to a local hub. The internet wasn’t commercially available yet, so the company basically built its own closed network, with centralized computers that maintained large databases and performed most of the calculations. Commands entered on the keyboard sent a request to the hub, which processed the information and sent back the result.  The Chiclet keyboard for the Bloomberg Terminal was introduced around 1983. Although it looks like a generic keyboard, its function keys were finance-specific hot keys.National Museum of American History/Smithsonian InstitutionHot keys let traders easily call up data on government securities, corporate debt, and currency markets, among other things. A series of keystrokes would pull up other historical and real-time data, run an analysis, or place a trade. Learning how to use the terminal and digest the vast amount of information, which was presented mostly in tabular form, became a rite of passage for users.In 1990, Bloomberg added a trackball to the keyboard, which helped the user navigate the multiple windows and menus typically displayed on screen. Two years later, the keyboard gained a built-in speaker, to support multimedia information; this design also included telephone, headphone, and microphone jacks. One of the most popular features was Instant Bloomberg, which allowed users to chat directly with fellow Bloomberg Terminal users over the proprietary network. By 1996, Bloomberg had keyboards that supported 23 different languages. In the early 2000s, the company began incorporating biometric authentication for terminal login, via a fingerprint reader on the keyboard.As the company’s business model evolved, the Bloomberg Terminal added services well beyond its initial offerings. In 1990, for example, worried that Dow Jones would stop providing access to its news stories, Bloomberg set up its own news service. It recruited Wall Street Journal reporter Matthew Winkler to oversee a dozen reporters; their stories on market and securities movements used graphs and calculations that served as advertisements for the terminal’s capabilities. These days, the Bloomberg news empire includes Bloomberg Businessweek, Bloomberg Radio, and Bloomberg Television.Bloomberg’s subscription-based financial model included the leasing of a Bloomberg Terminal with its specialized keyboard and other hardware, access to a dedicated private network, and a suite of services. In 1999, a subscription to a single Bloomberg Terminal cost $1,600 per month with a minimum two-year contract and a discount on each additional terminal. Today the annual price is upwards of $32,000 (trending a little below inflation). In 1995, the company launched a suite of “Open Bloomberg” software products that ran on the customer’s own PC; five years later, it stopped leasing dedicated terminals. Current customers also have access to mobile applications that allow terminal functions to run on phones and tablets. Today, “Bloomberg Terminal” has come to refer to the integrated data, analytics, news, communications, and trading environment.The Legacy of the Bloomberg TerminalAlthough the shift away from dedicated terminals was a logical response to the rise of the internet and publicly available market data, it altered the material culture of financial work. For nearly two decades, Bloomberg Terminals commanded an aura of power and financial prowess. They were emblems of market mastery, with a brand that was distinct from other office computers. With Open Bloomberg, users were no longer tied to a single desk or a fixed set of monitors.And so, cast-off Bloomberg Terminals found their way into museum collections. They’re a physical embodiment of the ethereal nature of financial markets, and a manifestation of mathematical calculations, network infrastructure, and business culture.  The Bloomberg keyboard used by “Bond King” Bill Gross has his login and password taped on the front.National Museum of American History/Smithsonian InstitutionThe Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of American History has a number of Bloomberg keyboards in its collection, but my favorite is object number 2014.0012.02, which was used by “Bond King” Bill Gross during the 1990s and 2000s at Pacific Investment Management. Gross had cofounded PIMCO in 1971 and built it into a $2 trillion bond investment firm. I especially love that Gross taped his login and password directly on his keyboard, which makes the object more relatable. I may never know what it’s like to manage billions in assets from a Bloomberg Terminal, but I absolutely understand the trial of remembering my passwords.Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.An abridged version of this article appears in the October 2026 print issue as “The Keyboard That Moved Markets.”ReferencesBloomberg Professional Services has a nice timeline showing the evolution of its keyboards.For an economic analysis of how computers like the Bloomberg Terminal changed financial markets, see Gerben Bakker’s 2025 paper “The Terminal Revolution: Reuters and Bloomberg as global providers of financial and economic news, 1960–2020,” published by the London School of Economics and Political Science.Bloomberg Terminals are in the collections of many museums, including the Computer History Museum and the National Museum of American History.

Climate & Environment.title: Electricity Theft Is Rampant, but Delhi Found a Fix
Climate & Environment.text: It’s disheartening how much power gets generated and then promptly lost as it travels through grid networks. This leaking of electricity happens when it vanishes as heat as well as when it is pilfered by thieves and nonpaying customers.  More than half of the countries that track these metrics lost at least 10 percent of their electricity in 2023, according to the World Bank. Losses topped 20 percent for 24 of those nations. Two countries lost more than half of what they generated.  With numbers this high, cutting down on losses makes sense. Electricity demand is rising beyond what many grid operators can supply; reducing waste would help meet some of that demand without having to build new power plants. Plus, when the power comes from fossil fuels, any loss means emitting even more greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. And electric losses hit the bottom lines of power providers, which ultimately pass those costs on to everyone else.  The trouble is, reducing electricity losses is a hard and expensive process that takes a long time. Typically, the less maintained the grid infrastructure, the more electricity that’s lost. And the more fragile the region’s law enforcement and government, the more prevalent the power theft. Natural disasters and war make things worse. Delhi’s Power Grid ComebackFixing a power grid requires a systemic approach across many sectors. There’s no one technology that will solve the problem. At the outset, the obstacles to success may feel insurmountable. Equipment across entire grid networks must be updated. Multiple arms of government must agree to reforms and coordinate to ensure power providers are set up to succeed. Regulations must be written or revised, investments made, cultures changed.The city of Delhi did all those things. Over the past 25 years, it cut its electricity losses from about 50 to 5 percent. How the city pulled off that impressive feat is the focus of “The Epic Comeback of Delhi’s Power Grid” by Mini Shaji Thomas, an electrical engineer at the university Jamia Millia Islamia who has lived in Delhi since the 1990s. She gives us a view from the inside—as a resident and a power systems expert.  Delhi is a shining example, but some other regions have significantly lowered electricity losses over the last quarter century too. The country of Georgia went from losses of over 16 percent in 2002 to about 8 percent in 2023. In Singapore, losses dropped from 6.6 percent to a nearly nonexistent 0.2 percent over the same time period. Global Electricity Theft CrisisBut there are many parts of the world where electricity losses remain a problem or have gotten worse. In Jamaica, where power theft is rampant, losses have hovered between 21 and 28 percent for years. Argentina’s losses nearly doubled between 2015 and 2023, going from an all-time low of about 12 percent to an all-time high of nearly 24 percent. The main problem: Transmission and distribution companies lacked the capital to maintain and upgrade their networks, which left equipment operating under stress. A delay in the installation of smart meters has allowed thieves to more easily siphon power and tamper with meters.  Thomas says she hopes her account of Delhi’s grid comeback will serve as a blueprint for others. It’s possible to replicate the sweeping changes Delhi made, she says. But it “requires a concerted effort from all stakeholders, customers, the utility, the government, and their employees.”

Entertainment.title: Joel Lyall Is Flipping His Daily Routine to Stay Ahead of the Fashion Game
Entertainment.text: “When everyone else has gone to bed, it always comes back to why I started this,” shares Joel Lyall. The stylist and founder of vintage streetwear boutique Bythepeace is busy unloading fresh stock from his car outside his studio in West London. “Six years ago, I was working from my brother’s room at night, staying motivated to get things done. Now, this time of day is a reminder to keep pushing and persevering.”Hypebeast links up with Lyall at the start of the evening for a new campaign with UGG. As the pace of the city slows down, he lets us into what he considers the peak of his working day. From ideating streetwear looks to preparing vintage garments for sale, the visuals capture how the stylist seizes new opportunities at nightfall, while kitted out in the brand’s functional yet fashion-forward Fall 2026 collection. "This time of day is a reminder to keep pushing and persevering."Surrounded by almost 70 pieces from various stockists, Lyall wastes no time in getting to work. “Sometimes I start by measuring and steaming the clothes, other times I note it all down on my spreadsheet, and that's just the beginning,” he shares. With his evening in full swing, the stylist relies on the UGG Birch Hiker for long-lasting comfort. A low-top, utilitarian shoe originating from the 1999 Birch Collection, the silhouette has been reworked with durable materials to support active lives like Lyall’s. As he mentions, organizing garments is just the beginning, so after separating them into what can be styled for upcoming projects or archived for future collections, he begins posting pieces to the website. “I upload around 9 p.m. whilst my customers are in bed and may be scrolling through what they can buy,” he explains. “People are especially active through the night, so that's when I can take advantage and get ahead of the game, making sure they see my items first.”At this point, Lyall switches to the UGG Birch Boot. Though it's built with a waterproof outer, the lightweight feel and sheepskin liner allow it to double up as a cozy indoor shoe. “I try to prioritize versatility and functionality throughout my day,” he says. Taking us through his outfit, the stylist explains, “I love wearing my blue denim and plain white T-shirt with the UGG boots; they can be styled in so many ways.” "I try to prioritize versatility and functionality, and with the UGG boots, they can be styled in so many ways."Wrapping up at the studio, Lyall keeps the Birch Boot on foot and heads home, where the energy of the day finally winds down. “The night is all about getting up and going, but after that, I like to take it slow,” he shares. “Refreshing your mind creatively is so important because I can get stimulated by everything. Being able to go home and have clear thinking is normally where most of my ideas come from.” View this post on InstagramA post shared by HYPEBEAST UK (@hypebeastuk) Explore the full campaign produced by Hypebeast in the galleries above. Entertainment.text: SummaryG-Shock has officially unveiled the MRG-D5000 featuring an outer case and bezel rendered entirely in synthetic blue sapphire crystalConceived by brand creator Kikuo Ibe in 2017 the shock-resistant timepiece required nearly a decade of technical developmentProduction is strictly limited to 20 pieces globally with each watch hand-assembled by a single master technician at Casio's Yamagata factoryCasio G-Shock has officially revealed the G-Shock MRG-D5000 Blue Sapphire, marking the most expensive production watch in the brand's history. Priced at $80,000 USD (£67,000 GBP), the record-setting model turns a long-standing concept envisioned by brand creator Kikuo Ibe in 2017 into an ultra-exclusive reality.Constructed entirely from lab-grown blue sapphire crystal across its outer case and bezel, the G-Shock MRG-D5000 measures 16.45mm in thickness to accommodate the material's structural requirements. To prevent fracturing without relying on traditional drill holes or screws, G-Shock engineered an interlocking assembly framework inspired by traditional Japanese timber joinery. Flipping the watch over reveals a Grade 5 titanium caseback set with sapphire crystal, engraved with "DREAM PROJECT" alongside its individual edition number from 1/20 to 20/20. Entertainment.title: Matières Fécales Presents "THE NINETY NINE PERCENT" SS27 Collection at Place de la République
Entertainment.text: SummaryMatières Fécales staged its SS27 runway presentation titled THE NINETY NINE PERCENT at Paris's Place de la RépubliqueDesigned by Steven Raj Bhaskaran alongside Hannah Rose the collection featured 99 looks modeled entirely by people of colorThe show highlighted a footwear collaboration with Christian Louboutin alongside hand-woven textiles from Burkina Faso and IndiaMatières Fécales has unveiled its Spring/Summer 2027 collection, titled "THE NINETY NINE PERCENT," staging the first-ever fashion show at the historic Place de la République during Paris Fashion Week. Conceived by designer Steven Raj Bhaskaran with support from creative partner Hannah Rose, the presentation served as a deeply personal manifesto honoring immigrant families, working-class communities, and marginalized identities through 99 looks modeled entirely by people of color.Structured across three distinct chapters—“FAMILY,” “TRIBE,” and “GODS”—the collection translates Bhaskaran's personal journey into elevated garments. The opening "FAMILY" segment introduced white draped ensembles, Thawb-inspired cotton dress shirts, hardware-accented silk trenches, and modest micro-pleated chiffon skirts. The section also debuted curved-heel flip-flop footwear created in collaboration with Christian Louboutin, closing with Bhaskaran walking the runway alongside his mother, sister, and niece.Transitioning into "TRIBE," the collection explored alternative youth culture with military tulle tweed sets, decaying lamb leather capes, metallic "Golden Touch" gloves, and heavy-duty "Stomper" combat boots. The final "GODS" section highlighted global artisanal techniques, featuring hand-woven cotton suits by Cabes Gie in Burkina Faso and hand-embroidered sarees by Tilfi in Varanasi, India, reimagined as decayed 1950s ball gowns. In a striking finale, models carried life-like billionaire figures around the République statue to Nina Simone’s "Tomorrow Is My Turn."A portion of sales from the Spring/Summer 2027 collection will directly support La Maison d’Allanah, a non-profit organization providing housing for LGBTQIA+ refugees in France.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Now reimagined and explicitly designed for life in orbit, the runner transitions from its competitive athletic origins into a contemporary footwear staple.In the newly revealed campaign imagery, LISA pairs the archival sneaker with a bold, red color-blocked ensemble. The styling emphasizes the shoe's low-profile construction, exposed traction elements, and classic vintage aesthetics. By bringing the 1971 design language back into clear view, the campaign successfully merges foundational athletic heritage with modern cultural relevance.The Nike Moon Shoe launches globally on October 1, 2026 via Nike. Longevity & Anti-Aging.text: Why is the APOEε2 variant of the APOE gene associated with a lower risk of Alzheimer's disease and slightly longer life expectancy? Past research has investigated the role of APOE in cholesterol metabolism and inflammation in microglia, the innate immune cells of the brain implicated in neurodegenerative conditions. Here, researchers focus instead on pericytes and their role in maintaining the blood-brain barrier. The barrier prevents unwanted molecules and cells from entering the brain, but becomes leaky with age. This leakage of the blood-brain barrier generates inflammation and damage in the brain, and is thought to be an early inciting event in the onset of neurodegenerative conditions.
